column2: Seeing that most wondrous sight, Drona's son, weaponless and tormented, spoke, remembering Kripa's words:

One who does not heed the unpleasant but beneficial words of friends grieves on meeting calamity, as I do, having gone against those two.
mahabharata:10:6.20	He who, transgressing, seeks to slay those declared in the scriptures not to be slain, falls from the path of dharma and takes a wrong road.
mahabharata:10:6.21	Against cows, Brahmanas, kings and women, a friend, a mother, a teacher, the aged, children, the dull and the blind, those asleep, afraid or just risen,
mahabharata:10:6.22	and the intoxicated, mad or careless, one should not take up weapons—so the elders taught men of old.
mahabharata:10:6.23	Having left the eternal road seen in the scriptures and begun by a wrong way, I have come to dreadful calamity.
mahabharata:10:6.24	The wise say that calamity is most dreadful when one, having raised up a great undertaking, turns back from it out of fear.
mahabharata:10:6.25	And who can do the impossible by the power of his strength? Human action is not said to be greater than fate.
mahabharata:10:6.26	If one performing a human act does not succeed through fate, he has fallen from the path of dharma and meets with calamity.
mahabharata:10:6.27	The wise call it an unknown obstruction when, having begun some act, one turns back from it here out of fear.
mahabharata:10:6.28	This fear that has come to me is from ill-conducted action; but Drona's son would never in any way turn back in battle.
mahabharata:10:6.29	And this very great being, raised like the rod of fate—though I think, I do not in any way recognise it.
mahabharata:10:6.30	Surely this stained purpose of mine, which turned to unrighteousness, shows this dreadful fruit as an obstruction.
mahabharata:10:6.31	This turning back of mine in battle was ordained by fate; there is no way to rise against fate here.
mahabharata:10:6.32	So today I take refuge in Mahadeva, the lord; he will destroy this dreadful rod of fate for me.
mahabharata:10:6.33	I take refuge in the matted-haired god of gods, lord of Uma, garlanded with skulls, Rudra, Hara, destroyer of Bhaga's eyes.
mahabharata:10:6.34	That god surpassed the gods by austerity and prowess; therefore I shall go for refuge to Girisha, trident in hand.
[Drona's son said:] "The fierce Sthanu, Shiva, Rudra, Sharva, Ishana, Ishvara, Girisha, the boon-giving god, Bhava, the imperishable creator of beings,
the blue-throated, unborn, Shakra, Kratha, destroyer of sacrifice, Hara, of universal form, of strange eyes, of many forms, lord of Uma,
dweller in cremation grounds, proud, great lord of hosts, bearer of the skull-topped staff, shaven, matted, celibate:
with my mind, though hard to attain and of little understanding, I, offering my own self, will worship the slayer of Tripura.
The praised, the praiseworthy, who is being praised, the unfailing, clad in hide, the dark red, the blue-throated, the unseparated, the irresistible,
the bright, the creator of the universe, Brahma and the celibate, firm in vows, ever in austerity, endless, refuge of ascetics,
of many forms, lord of hosts, three-eyed, dear to his retinue, with face watched by the lords of hosts, beloved of Gauri's heart,
father of Kumara, tawny, with a noble bull as his vehicle, lightly clad, most fierce, intent on adorning Uma,
the god in golden armour, adorned with the moon in his crest—I take refuge in the god with supreme concentration.
I shall cross this dreadful calamity today, so hard to cross; with an offering of all beings I shall, pure, worship the pure one."
Knowing this resolve of his, his mind inclined to self-sacrifice, a golden altar appeared before that great soul.
On that altar, O king, a fire arose, filling the sky, the quarters, the intermediate quarters and space with its flames.
And there appeared many with blazing mouths and eyes, with many feet, heads and arms, huge-mouthed, like elephants and mountains.
Some in forms of dogs, boars and camels, with faces of horses, jackals and cows, bears and cats, tigers and leopards,
with crow faces, frog faces, parrot faces, with great python faces and swan faces, of white lustre,
with woodpecker faces and chasha faces, Bharata, with tortoise and crocodile faces and dolphin faces,
with great makara faces and timi faces, with monkey faces, krauncha faces, with pigeon and elephant faces,
with dove faces, with madgu faces, with hands for ears, thousand-eyed, hundred-bellied,
fleshless, with kokila faces and hawk faces, Bharata, headless ones, O king, and bear-faced, terrifying,
with blazing eyes and tongues, with faces of flame, with ram faces, and others, king, with goat faces,
shell-coloured, with shell faces, with shell ears, wearing garlands of shells, with a sound like the blowing of a conch,
matted-haired, five-crested, shaven, thin-bellied, four-tusked, four-tongued, spike-eared, crowned,
wearing crests, O king, with curled hair, turbaned, crowned, fair-faced, well adorned,
wearing garlands of lotuses and blue lotuses, bearing kumudas, endowed with greatness, by hundreds and thousands.
With shataghnis and discuses in hand, with pestles, bhushundis and nooses, and maces in hand, Bharata,
quivers bound on their backs, with wondrous arrows, fierce in battle, with banners and flags, with bells and axes,
with great nooses raised in their hands, with clubs in hand, with posts in hand, with swords, with serpents raised as crests, wearing great serpents as armlets and wondrous ornaments,
dust-stained and mud-smeared, all garlanded with white garments, blue-limbed and lotus-limbed, with shaven faces,
the delighted retainers, golden-lustred, played kettledrums, conches, mridangas, jharjharas, anakas and gomukhas.
Some sang, others danced, others leapt and sprang, the mighty ones, and others pranced.
Running, swift and fierce, their hair tossed by the wind, roaring again and again like rutting great elephants,
very dreadful and of fearful form, with spears and pattishas in hand, in garments of many colours, with wondrous garlands and unguents,
wearing armlets set with many jewels, with hands raised, slayers of foes, heroes of irresistible and unbearable valour,
drinkers of blood and fat and others, eating meat and entrails, crested, ear-ringed, very lean, pot-bellied,
very short and very tall, very strong and very dreadful, huge, with lips hanging like Death's, with large organs and lumps of bone,
with costly many-formed crowns, others shaven or matted, who could make the sky, with its sun, moon, planets and stars, fall on the earth,
who could slay the fourfold host of beings, who are ever fearless, the warriors of Hara's frown,
doers at will, the perfected, lords of the lords of the three worlds, ever in joy and delight, masters of speech, free of envy,
who having attained the eightfold lordship feel no pride, whose deeds ever amaze the revered Hara,
who have ever worshipped him with mind, speech and action in devotion, whom he guards with mind, speech and action as devotees, like his own sons,
others who drink blood and fat, ever angry at the haters of Brahmanas, who ever drink the twenty-four-fold soma,
who by learning, celibacy, austerity and self-control, having worshipped the trident-marked one, have attained union with Bhava,
the revered Maheshvara, with Parvati and these, his own selves, enjoys with the hosts of beings, the lord of the past, present and future.
With various wondrous laughter, slapping of arms, shouts and roars, making the universe resound, they approached Ashvatthaman,
praising Mahadeva, shining brilliantly, wishing to increase the glory of the great-souled son of Drona.
Wishing to know his energy and to see the night attack, with dreadful bludgeons, firebrands, spears and pattishas in hand, hosts of spirits of terrible form gathered on every side.
Though they could cause fear to the three worlds by their very sight, looking at them the mighty one felt no distress.
Then Drona's son, bow in hand, with his iguana-skin fingerguard tied on, offered himself, by himself, as the offering.
The bows were the firewood there, the sharp arrows the purifying grass, and the soul-controlled self the oblation in that rite, Bharata.
Then, with a gentle mantra, the mighty Drona's son, filled with great wrath, offered himself as the oblation.
Praising the great-souled Rudra of terrible deeds, unfallen, by terrible acts, he said with joined palms:

Born in the family of Angiras, I offer this self into the fire today, revered one; accept me as the offering.
mahabharata:10:7.55	Out of devotion to you, Mahadeva, with supreme concentration, soul of the universe, I offer myself before you in this calamity.
mahabharata:10:7.56	In you all beings abide, and you abide in all beings; the unity of the chief qualities rests in you.
mahabharata:10:7.57	Lord, who dwell in the hearts of all beings, the oblation has come before you; accept me, god, since foes cannot be overcome by me otherwise.
Having said this, Drona's son mounted that altar with its blazing fire and, giving up himself, climbed up and sat in the fire.
Seeing him with arms raised, motionless, present as an oblation, the revered Mahadeva himself said, as if laughing:

By truth, purity, uprightness, renunciation, austerity, restraint, forbearance, devotion, steadfastness, wisdom and speech,
mahabharata:10:7.61	I have been duly worshipped by Krishna of untroubled deeds; therefore no one is dearer to me than Krishna.
mahabharata:10:7.62	Honouring him and wishing to test you, I suddenly protected the Panchalas and worked many illusions.
mahabharata:10:7.63	This honour was done to him by me in protecting the Panchalas; but they are overcome by Time; there is no life for them today.
Having said this, the revered one entered the body of the great archer, his own form, and gave him an excellent, spotless sword.
Then, entered by the revered one, he blazed again with splendour and in battle became formidable by the energy created by the god.
Unseen beings and Rakshasas surrounded him as he went toward the enemy's camp, like the Lord himself.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Surely the two were not stopped by the petty guards, nor noticed, nor did the two great chariot-warriors turn back thinking it unbearable?
Did they crush the camp, slay the Somakas and Pandavas, and reach Duryodhana's supreme path in the battle?
Or were they slain by the Panchalas, did they not lie on the ground? What did the two do? Tell me, Sanjaya."
[Sanjaya said:] When the great-souled Drona's son had gone toward the camp, Kripa and Kritavarman stood at the camp gate.
Seeing the two great chariot-warriors alert, Ashvatthaman, glad, slowly said these words, O king:

You two, alert, are enough for the destruction of the whole kshatriya order, how much more of the remnant of warriors, asleep especially.
mahabharata:10:8.8	I shall enter the camp and roam like Death, so that no man escapes me alive.
Having said this, Drona's son entered the great camp of the Parthas, by no gate, assaulting it, casting off his own fear.
Having done a great deed and being greatly tired in the battle, they slept in full trust, surrounded by their own troops.
Then, entering the dwelling of Dhrishtadyumna, Bharata, Drona's son saw the Panchala asleep on his bed close by.
On a great bed of white silk, covered with a rich coverlet, adorned with the finest garlands, perfumed with incense and powders,
he woke that great soul, lying confident and fearless, with his foot, O king, as he lay on the bed.
Waking at the touch of the foot, the immeasurable one, mad for battle, rose and recognised Drona's son, the great chariot-warrior.
As he rose from the bed, mighty Ashvatthaman seized him by the hair and crushed him to the ground with his hands.
Crushed by that strong one, and by fear and sleep, Bharata, the Panchala could not move then.
Mounting him then, O king, on his throat and chest, he killed him, roaring and struggling, like a beast of sacrifice.
Clawing at Drona's son with his nails, he said indistinctly: "Son of my teacher, kill me with a weapon, do not delay; by you may I go to the worlds of merit, best of men."
Hearing his indistinct words, Drona's son said: "There are no worlds for slayers of a teacher, defiler of your family; therefore you do not deserve death by weapon, evil-minded one."
As he spoke thus, like a lion a rutting elephant, in rage he struck that hero on his vitals with his terrible heels.
At the cries of that hero being killed in the dwelling, the women and his guards awoke, great king.
Seeing that huge, superhumanly valiant figure, they took it for a ghost and did not speak out of fear.
Having sent him by that means to Yama's abode, the radiant one mounted his chariot and stood at the Sudarshana.
Leaving his dwelling, O king, making the quarters resound, the mighty one went by chariot to the camp, wishing to slay his foes.
When Drona's son, the great chariot-warrior, had gone, the women cried out with all those guards.
Seeing the king slain, sunk deep in grief, all the kshatriyas, Bharata, cried out for Dhrishtadyumna.
At their cry, the bulls among kshatriyas nearby quickly armed themselves, saying, "What is this?"
The frightened women, looking at the son of Bharadvaja, said in piteous voices: "Run quickly!
Whether Rakshasa or man, we know not; he who has slain the Panchala king stands mounted on a chariot."
Then the foremost warriors suddenly surrounded him; he struck down all of them as they rushed on with the Rudra weapon.
Having slain Dhrishtadyumna and his followers, he saw Uttamaujas asleep on his bed nearby.
Mounting him too, on the throat and chest with force, he likewise killed that roaring subduer of foes.
Yudhamanyu came up, thinking him killed by a Rakshasa, and, raising his mace, struck Drona's son on the chest with speed.
Rushing at him, he seized him, threw him to the ground, and as he struggled killed him like a beast.
Having thus slain him, the hero rushed at others, great chariot-warriors asleep here and there, O king, quivering and trembling like beasts at a sacrifice before the slaughterer.
Then, taking his sword, skilled in sword-fighting, he killed others, ordinary men, moving by separate paths.
Likewise, seeing in the barracks the sleeping men in the midst of the detachments, weary, with weapons laid down, he struck them all down in a moment.
With his excellent sword he cut down warriors, horses and elephants, all his limbs smeared with blood, like Death sent by Time.
By their struggles and by the swinging of his sword, Drona's son, with the cuts of the sword, became threefold bloodstained.
Drenched in blood, with blazing sword, fighting, his form seemed inhuman and exceedingly terrible.
Even those who were awake, Kaurava, bewildered by the noise, looking at one another and seeing Drona's son, were seized with trembling.
Seeing that form of his, the kshatriyas, tormentors of foes, thinking him a Rakshasa, closed their eyes.
He, of dreadful form, roamed the camp like Death, and saw the sons of Draupadi and the remaining Somakas.

Frightened by that noise, the great chariot-warriors, bows in hand, the sons of Draupadi, hearing that Dhrishtadyumna was slain, lord of men, fearlessly covered Bharadvaja's son with showers of arrows.
Then the Prabhadrakas, awakened by that cry, and Shikhandin harassed Drona's son with arrows.
Seeing them raining showers of arrows, the son of Bharadvaja roared a great roar, wishing to slay those hard-to-conquer foes.
Then, greatly enraged, remembering his father's slaying, he descended swiftly from the chariot and rushed at them.
Taking in the battle a broad shield with a thousand moons and a broad divine sword adorned with gold, the mighty one rushed at the sons of Draupadi and roamed with his sword.
Then that tiger among men struck Pratibindhya in the battle on the flank, O king, and he fell slain to the ground.
Sutasoma, mighty, pierced Drona's son with a lance and, raising his sword again, rushed at him.
The bull among men cut off Sutasoma's arm with the sword and struck him again on the side, and he fell, his heart split.
Shatanika, Nakula's son, valiant, lifted up a chariot-wheel with both arms and struck Drona's son on the chest.
The Brahmana struck Shatanika, who had let go of the wheel; he fell dazed to the ground, and then he took off his head.
Shrutakarma, taking a bludgeon, struck at Drona's son and rushed at him, hitting the left side of his shield hard.
He struck Shrutakarma in the mouth with the best of swords, and he fell slain to the ground, bewildered, his face distorted.
At that noise the hero Shrutakirti, great archer, approached Ashvatthaman and covered him with showers of arrows.
Warding off his showers of arrows with his shield, he cut off his shining head, with its earrings, from his body.
Then the slayer of Bhishma (Shikhandin), with all the Prabhadrakas, struck the hero on every side with various weapons and pierced him between the brows with an arrow.
The mighty son of Drona, filled with rage, reached Shikhandin and cut him in two with the sword.
Having slain Shikhandin, the scorcher of foes, filled with rage, rushed swiftly at all the Prabhadraka bands, and at whatever force of Virata remained.
The mighty one made dreadful slaughter of the sons, grandsons and friends of Drupada, seeing them each time.
Rushing at one man after another, Drona's son, skilled in the ways of the sword, cut them down with it.
They saw Kali, red-mouthed and red-eyed, wearing red garlands and unguents and red garments, alone, noose in hand, Shikhandini.
They saw Kalaratri standing smiling, binding men, horses and elephants with dreadful nooses and departing, carrying off various dead, bound by nooses, with hair loosened.
In dreams on other nights, lord, those chief warriors saw her leading away the sleeping, and Drona's son ever slaying.
From the time that the battle between the Kuru and Pandava armies began, they saw that Kritya and Drona's son too.
Those struck down earlier by fate, Drona's son felled afterwards, terrifying all beings, roaring dreadful roars.
Remembering that earlier vision, those heroes, afflicted by fate, thought, "This is that."
Then at that cry, hundreds and thousands of bowmen in the Pandava camp awoke.
He cut off the feet of one, the hips of another, split some in the sides, like Death sent by Time.
The earth, lord, was strewn with those crushed by the very fierce, roaring, greatly afflicted, and others trampled by elephants and horses.
As they cried out, "What is this? Who is this? What is the noise? What has been done?", Drona's son became their Death.
The best of strikers, Drona's son, sent the Pandava and Srinjaya warriors, enraged, stripped of weapons and armour, to the world of death.
Then, terrified by those weapons, rising up in fear, blind with sleep and bereft of their senses, they hid here and there.
Seized by stiffness of the thighs, their strength struck down by faintness, crying aloud in great fear, they crushed one another.
Then Drona's son, again mounting the chariot of dreadful rumble, bow in hand, sent others with arrows to Yama's abode.
Some of the best men leaping up again even from afar, and other heroes rushing on, he offered to Kalaratri.
Likewise, with the front of his chariot, crushing, he ran about, and then rained showers of arrows of many kinds on his enemies.
And again with the wondrous shield of a hundred moons, of sky colour, he roamed with his sword.
Thus Drona's son, mad for battle, agitated their camp, O king of kings, as an elephant a great lake.
At that noise the warriors, O king, rose senseless, oppressed by sleep and fear, and ran here and there.
Others cried out in discordant voices, speaking incoherently; they could not find their weapons or clothes.
Others with hair loosened did not know one another; some, frightened, rose and wandered about; some voided excrement, some passed urine.
Horses and elephants, breaking their bonds, O king of kings, fell upon others together, making great confusion.
There some men, afraid, hid on the ground, and elephants and horses crushed them as they lay.
While this went on, bull among men, the Rakshasas, satisfied, bellowed loudly in joy, best of the Bharatas.
That sound, sent up by the hosts of beings in joy, filled all the quarters and even the sky with a great noise.
Hearing their cries of distress, the terrified elephants and horses broke loose, O king, and ran about trampling the people in the camp.
The dust raised by their feet as they ran about there made the darkness of the night in their camp twofold.
When that darkness fell, the people everywhere were bewildered; fathers did not know sons, nor brothers brothers.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, hundreds of sons and wives, have been experienced in the cycles of existence—whose are they to you, or you to them?
How could the kshatriya go to heaven, purified by weapons, lord? Therefore the Creator made the maiden's womb as a source of conflict.
Whatever states there are, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, all of them, having Time as their nature, are set in motion in creatures.
Perform, Yudhishthira, king of kings, the Rajasuya, the Ashvamedha, the Sarvamedha and the Naramedha, Bharata.
No man, out of fear, ever said anything ill of King Dhritarashtra or of Duryodhana in Yudhishthira's hearing.
This too has come to pass, what Yudhishthira said of old, seeing most dreadful portents when the armies were arrayed.
The princess did no unrighteous act, scorcher of foes; what then, O king, is the reason that Krishna (Draupadi) fell to the earth?
He saw a river filled with hot water, very hard to cross, and a forest of sword-leaves set with sharp razors.
